case_study_insert.main_stem: Tideway Rail Logistics (TRL) is a private limited company in the rail freight and container transport sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2008 by Grace Whitfield, TRL moves bulk goods for manufacturers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership to meet tight timetables. TRL plans to invest $960,000 in new freight wagons and a digital yard-management system, financed by $560,000 of hire purchase and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $15.00 a unit and a selling price of $25.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. Absenteeism has reached 11% and retailer quality complaints are rising, threatening TRL's reliability on key routes.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — June 2025: TRL ran 9,200 freight trains last quarter with a wagon defect rate of 2.1%, down from 3.6% a year ago. On-time arrivals reached 88% while quality complaints fell from 51 to 29 a month. Average yard turnaround is 4.2 hours. A survey of 250 staff found that 66% wanted a punctuality bonus and 61% felt absenteeism was their team's biggest problem. Records show 16 of 80 drivers need refresher signalling training; on-the-job training is run at the depot and off-the-job courses at the rail academy cost $820 per driver.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Tideway Rail Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (February 2027): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising the cost of TRL's hire-purchase agreement. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $14.00 to $14.90 an hour, increasing the wage bill for depot and train crew. (3) Diesel and rail-part input costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, while freight inflation is 5.2% and manufacturing output grew 2.6%.

questions.question_text: TRL is funding wagons through hire purchase. Explain two advantages for TRL of using hire purchase rather than a conventional bank loan for this $960,000 expansion.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the cost of the $560,000 wagon investment over the life of the asset, so TRL does not need to find a large lump sum and can keep its $400,000 retained profit for working capital. Fixed costs are already $600,000 a year and the base rate has risen to 5.00%, so predictable instalments make cash-flow planning easier for a business whose 88% on-time record depends on reliable wagons. The wagons are used as security, which can make finance easier to obtain than an unsecured loan.

Point 2: Hire purchase preserves borrowing capacity for other needs. Because the agreement is asset-linked, TRL keeps more of its credit headroom than if it borrowed the full amount, which helps if the 11% absenteeism and rising quality complaints require extra spending on training or maintenance. Under hire purchase the firm also obtains use of the wagons immediately, so it can start serving the 2.6% growth in manufacturing output straight away and earn the $10.00 contribution per unit while paying over time. Ownership transfers at the end, which suits a long-term rail operator.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of hire purchase over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TRL's expansion, financing and operations.

questions.question_text: TRL is tendering for new manufacturing contracts. Consider national newspaper advertising, trade journal advertising, or social media marketing. Which should TRL choose to win these contracts? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National newspaper advertising: A newspaper campaign gives TRL wide, fast reach and can raise its profile with senior managers across many regions, which supports the $960,000 wagon investment. However, newspapers are expensive and most readers are not buyers of bulk rail freight, so wastage is high for an 80-employee operator with fixed costs of $600,000. The 2.6% growth in manufacturing output is concentrated among specific firms, not a general audience.

Trade journal advertising: Rail-freight and logistics journals reach exactly the procurement managers who award contracts, at a fraction of newspaper cost, and can carry technical detail about the digital yard-management system, the 88% on-time record and the falling 2.1% defect rate. Limitations are a narrower readership and monthly publication, meaning slow campaign response, but the audience quality is high.

Social media marketing: Targeted posts can highlight reliability figures and new wagons cheaply and can be updated quickly, with measurable engagement. Yet conversion from social clicks to large freight tenders is slow and uncertain, and the 66% of staff wanting a punctuality bonus is an internal rather than a customer message.

Recommendation: TRL should choose trade journal advertising. It reaches the manufacturing logistics managers who decide contracts, fits the $560,000 hire-purchase budget, and can present the service and technical improvements that matter. Newspaper advertising is rejected as costly and untargeted for a specialist operator; social media alone is rejected because it rarely secures large industrial tenders, so it should only reinforce the trade campaign. Because the 2.6% growth in manufacturing output is concentrated among identifiable firms, a trade title offers the most efficient route to those decision-makers, and the 88% punctuality record gives a concrete message to carry.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal reference to TRL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to TRL and partial judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in TRL's context with a clear recommendation explaining why newspaper and social-media-only options are rejected.

questions.question_text: TRL's absenteeism has reached 11% and retailer quality complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for TRL of its autocratic leadership in tackling these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets founder Grace Whitfield set clear, consistent standards and act quickly when reliability slips, which suits a hierarchical structure and tight rail timetables. With absenteeism at 11%, management can redeploy staff and enforce punctuality rules immediately rather than waiting for consultation, protecting the 88% on-time arrival record and the 2.1% wagon defect rate that underpin retailer contracts.

Point 2: Centralised decisions give rapid, uniform responses to the rising quality complaints. A single clear directive on inspection routines can be applied across the 9,200 monthly trains, reducing variation that causes complaints and shortening the 4.2-hour yard turnaround. Clear direction also makes it easier to tell the 16 drivers needing refresher signalling training what is required, so the $820 per-driver courses deliver measurable improvement. This style is effective in a safety-critical, time-bound operation, though TRL should watch that strict control does not worsen the 61% of staff who see absenteeism as their team's main problem.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of autocratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TRL's absenteeism, complaints and timetable.

questions.question_text: TRL must train the 16 drivers needing refresher signalling training. Consider on-the-job training at the depot or off-the-job courses at the rail academy. Which should TRL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the depot and on TRL's own wagons is directly relevant to the yard-management system and signalling routines, costs no fees, and keeps drivers available, protecting the 9,200 monthly trains and the 88% on-time record. Trainers can demonstrate the exact checks that keep the 2.1% defect rate low and that reduce quality complaints. Drawbacks are that trainers are working drivers whose own duties suffer, bad habits may be copied, and there is no external accreditation, which may matter for safety-sensitive contracts.

Off-the-job courses: The rail academy charges $820 per driver, so training the 16 drivers would cost $13,120 (16 × $820), minor against the $960,000 wagon programme. Courses provide structured, up-to-date signalling content and a recognised certificate, supporting safety and the 66% of staff who want clear standards. However, drivers are away from the depot, risking the 4.2-hour yard turnaround, and generic course material may not mirror TRL's specific yard layout.

Decision: TRL should choose off-the-job courses for the 16 drivers, followed by depot coaching. The recognised qualification best supports safety and reliability when absenteeism is 11%, and $13,120 is affordable; on-the-job training alone is rejected because it cannot certify signalling competence and may pass on local shortcuts, whereas the academy course gives a consistent standard TRL can rely on. The qualification also supports recruitment and retention while absenteeism is 11% and 16 drivers need updating, and it gives retailer customers evidence of competence as complaints remain a concern. To protect the 9,200 monthly trains and the 4.2-hour yard turnaround, TRL should schedule the 16 places in small groups and follow each course with depot coaching on its own signalling layout.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TRL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods with reference to TRL's costs and operations.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in TRL's context with a justified decision covering safety, cost and disruption.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TRL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $600,000 ÷ ($25.00 − $15.00) = $600,000 ÷ $10.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $25.00 − $15.00 = $10.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $10.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TRL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 60,000-unit break-even output with 100,000 units actually delivered gives a margin of safety of 40,000 units, confirming capacity to service the $960,000 wagon investment even if 11% absenteeism disrupts operations.
2. Contribution of $10.00 a unit lets managers model a price cut to win manufacturing contracts: a hypothetical $1.00 reduction would lower contribution to $9.00 and raise break-even to $600,000 ÷ $9.00 = 66,666.67 units, showing the extra volume required.
3. With fixed costs of $600,000, managers can set the volume needed to meet hire-purchase instalments and check it against the 9,200 trains run each quarter before adding more wagons.
4. Unit cost of $21.00 ($600,000 ÷ 100,000 units = $6.00 fixed cost per unit, plus $15.00 variable cost) can be monitored against the 8.9% diesel and rail-part inflation, while labour productivity of 100,000 units ÷ 80 staff = 1,250 units per worker helps measure the effect of absenteeism and quality complaints.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 40,000 units vs 100,000 output; price-cut modelling vs $600,000 fixed costs; instalment-cover volume target; and unit-cost benchmarking at $21.00 with productivity of 1,250 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TRL's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has TRL's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 38.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue of $6,000,000 in 2024 less cost of sales of $3,900,000 gives gross profit of $2,100,000; revenue of $6,800,000 in 2025 less $4,216,000 gives $2,584,000. Gross profit divided by revenue yields 35.0% and 38.0%. Operating profit of $750,000 in 2024 and $1,020,000 in 2025, each divided by revenue, yields 12.5% and 15.0%. Operating profit divided by capital employed of $5,000,000 and $6,000,000 yields 15.0% and 17.0%.

Evaluation: All three measures moved favourably. The first margin rose from 35.0% to 38.0%, meaning TRL held more of each revenue dollar after direct costs despite the 8.9% rise in diesel and rail-part costs, which is consistent with the falling 2.1% wagon defect rate. The overall margin improved from 12.5% to 15.0%, showing better overhead absorption as revenue grew by $800,000, helped by complaints falling from 51 to 29 a month. The return on capital increased from 15.0% to 17.0%; although capital employed rose to $6,000,000, operating profit grew by 36%, so the new wagons are adding value. Interest payable fell from $140,000 to $130,000, easing the burden of the $560,000 hire-purchase commitment and the higher base rate.

Conclusion: TRL's profitability has improved. Every ratio rose together, supported by higher revenue and gross profit and by lower interest costs, so the gain is broad-based rather than a one-off. The caution is that 11% absenteeism and rising complaints could still erode the 38.0% margin, so management should protect the improvement with the 16 driver training places and by monitoring diesel costs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or directional changes with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Correctly calculates the three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios for both years with detailed evaluation of margins, capital use and financing and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TRL of introducing a punctuality bonus for its drivers.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A punctuality bonus targets the 66% of 250 surveyed staff who want one and can raise motivation, reducing the 11% absenteeism that disrupts the 9,200 monthly trains. Better punctuality supports the 88% on-time arrival record and helps answer the rising retailer quality complaints, protecting the $10.00 contribution per unit and TRL's ability to win contracts as manufacturing output grows 2.6%.

Disadvantage: The bonus increases labour costs, and the insert gives no driver pay or hours, so its total cost cannot be quantified honestly. With the minimum wage set to rise 6.4% to $14.90 an hour and fixed costs of $600,000, an added bonus squeezes margins. It may also encourage drivers to skip safety checks to hit timetables, risking the 2.1% wagon defect rate, and could cause resentment if delays are outside a driver's control. There is also a risk that the bonus rewards factors drivers cannot influence, such as network congestion, which would demotivate the 61% of staff who already identify absenteeism as their team's biggest problem. Rather than a blanket payment, TRL should link any bonus to the 88% on-time target and the 2.1% defect rate, and the insert gives no cost figure to judge affordability against $600,000 fixed costs.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using TRL's survey, costs and service data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 8.9% rise in diesel and rail-part costs will affect TRL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): TRL's $560,000 hire-purchase agreement is explicitly exposed to the base rate, so a 0.75-point rise adds about 0.75% of $560,000 = $4,200 a year (0.0075 × $560,000) if the rate is variable. Against fixed costs of $600,000 this is modest, and $400,000 of retained profit was also used, so new borrowing is limited. Higher rates could still raise future finance costs and slow the 2.6% manufacturing growth, but the direct effect is small and can be hedged by fixing terms.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.90 an hour): Depot and train-crew roles are largely hourly paid, so wage costs rise at a time when 11% absenteeism and 16 drivers need retraining. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage bill can be invented; the honest test is given productivity of 100,000 units ÷ 80 staff = 1,250 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if absenteeism lowers output, unit labour cost rises and the $10.00 contribution per unit falls.

Input cost inflation (8.9% diesel and rail parts): The $15.00 variable cost per unit is exposed to diesel and parts, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the entire variable cost rose 8.9%, that would add 8.9% × $15.00 = $1.34 per unit, and across 100,000 units that is about $133,500 a year (100,000 × $1.34). Even a $0.75-per-unit rise would cost $75,000 a year. TRL can offset some of this through price discussions with manufacturers as output grows.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in diesel and rail-part costs will have the greatest impact. It repeats on every one of the 100,000 units, directly erodes the $10.00 contribution that supports the $960,000 wagon programme, and cannot be removed by a quick contractual fix. The interest effect is small and manageable, and the wage rise is serious but depends on unstated hours and on productivity TRL can influence, so both rank behind input inflation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to TRL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on TRL's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
